title: Mitosis and Meiosis Compared
short: Mitosis: one division, two identical diploid cells, for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, four different haploid cells, with crossing over and independent assortment.
trouble: Students mix the outcomes, such as four identical cells or two haploid cells. Count the divisions and ask what separates: homologs (only in meiosis I) or sister chromatids.

blocks.html: You have now seen both ways a eukaryotic cell divides its nucleus: Mitosis and Meiosis. Putting them side by side is the quickest way to keep them straight.
Mitosis: one division, two identical diploid cells, for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, four different haploid cells, with crossing over and independent assortment.

cards.text: Homologous pairs line up in the middle

blocks.html: One question sorts almost everything: what separates? If sister chromatids separate in the only division, the copies are shared out evenly and the daughters are identical (mitosis). If homologs separate first, each daughter gets one of each pair, half the number, and a different mix (meiosis I), and then the chromatids separate (meiosis II).

blocks.title: Predict the products
blocks.q: A cell with $2n = 12$ divides. Give the number of cells and the chromosomes in each (a) after mitosis, (b) after meiosis.
steps: (a) Mitosis: 2 cells, each with the parent's number, 12.

blocks.html: Mixing the outcomes, such as "four identical cells" or "two haploid cells". Neither division makes those. Count the divisions (one or two) and ask what separates (homologs separate only in meiosis I). One division of sister chromatids gives two identical diploid cells; two divisions starting with homologs give four different haploid cells. Check with humans: mitosis turns one cell of 46 into two cells of 46, and meiosis turns one cell of 46 into four cells of 23.
